summary:
Balam is an interactive web tool that helps mission planners evaluate and compare landing sites and dates near the Moon's south pole. At the pole, the Sun skims the horizon, Earth barely rises above it, and some craters never see light. A site that looks good on a map can turn out to be dark or cut off from Earth on the date that matters.

Balam combines NASA LOLA elevation data and SPICE ephemerides. For each site it builds a 360° horizon profile, then follows the Sun and Earth hour by hour across the mission window. The output is how long the site gets sunlight for solar power, when it has Direct-to-Earth communication, and how steep and rough the terrain is. All of this rolls up into a clear GO / NO-GO verdict with its reasons. Results appear on a 3D lunar globe, with permanently shadowed regions marked. A timeline slider lets you scrub through light and shadow, and several sites or dates can be compared side by side.

Choosing where and when to land decides whether a mission has power and contact with Earth. Balam turns complex NASA data into answers that are fast, visual and easy to explain.
details:
Balam

The problem we set out to solve

The Moon's south pole is the next great destination for exploration. Artemis and commercial missions are heading there because its permanently shadowed craters may hold water ice. Yet the pole is also one of the most complex places in the Solar System to plan a landing. The Sun never climbs high: it skims the horizon and casts long shadows across the terrain. Earth sits only a few degrees above the horizon, so a crater rim or a ridge can cut off the radio link. A site that looks ideal on a map could be in complete darkness, or unable to communicate with Earth, on the very days the mission needs it. A mistake here would leave the lander without power or without communications. Today, answering the question "where and when should we land?" means combining large topographic datasets, planetary ephemerides and specialized software. Balam was created to deliver that answer quickly, visually and in a way that is easy to explain.

What it does and how it works

Balam is an interactive web tool for planning lunar landings as quickly and efficiently as possible. After you choose a site and a date and press "Run simulation", Balam answers three questions: will there be sunlight to generate power? Will there be a direct radio link with Earth? Is the terrain safe to land on?. The answer comes as a GO, CAUTION or NO-GO verdict, with the measured value and threshold behind every reason.

The system has three interconnected components:

  • Mission console (React, TypeScript): Glass panels are layered over the lunar globe. A timeline slider replays the entire mission in memory at 60 fps, with no network calls, so light and shadow move across the terrain as you drag it. The Compare feature evaluates 2 to 5 scenarios (sites and dates) side by side. The History and Missions sections keep earlier work. A terrain detail view shows a 12 km area with its real slopes and shadows.


  • 3D lunar globe (CesiumJS): A Moon built from NASA data. The Moon you see in Balam is based entirely on NASA data, rendered as faithfully to reality as possible. Surface imagery comes from the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LROC, via NASA Moon Trek). Every hill, crater and ridge comes from the LRO laser altimeter (LOLA), at 40 meters per pixel at the south pole, served as terrain tiles from our own system. The positions of the Sun and Earth are calculated with NASA JPL ephemerides (SPICE). As a result, the lighting and horizon you see are exactly what a lander would face on that specific date. Nothing shown about the lunar surface or the geometry of the sky is invented or merely decorative.
    Short stays, a full lunar day or a complete lunar cycle. Missions can be simulated over 7 days, 14 days (about one lunar day at the pole) or a full 29.5-day lunar cycle covering both day and night. A short stay may look ideal, but a full cycle reveals when the site falls into darkness or loses sight of Earth. That information is crucial for any mission that must survive the lunar night.
    The Sun, Earth and stars are drawn in their real positions. Landing sites are color-coded by verdict, and permanently shadowed regions (PSRs) are outlined. The interface flies to the selected site and lights it according to the calculated position of the Sun. You can also switch to a view from the lander's perspective, showing the real horizon, or play a landing sequence featuring the lander and an astronaut.

  • Physics engine (Python, FastAPI): It uses NASA LOLA elevation models, at 40 m and 80 m per pixel over the south pole, and JPL SPICE kernels to determine the positions of the Sun and Earth. For each site it builds a 360° horizon profile from the real terrain, taking into account crater rims, ridges and the curvature of the Moon itself. It then analyzes the mission step by step, hour by hour, across the selected mission window (14 days by default). At each step it checks whether the Sun and Earth are above that horizon, accounting for lunar libration.
    This is essential because at the pole Earth never rises more than about 6° above the horizon. From this data it estimates the solar energy a sun-tracking panel could collect and gives a verdict: GO, CAUTION or NO-GO. Each verdict includes the measured values and their thresholds for slope, share of time in sunlight and availability of Direct-to-Earth contact. A PostGIS database stores 13 curated sites (10 candidate landing sites at the south pole and 3 Apollo sites for reference), 1,531 permanently shadowed regions (PSRs) and the results of previous simulations.

Around that core, the web app offers a complete planning workspace:

Simulate: plan a landing

  • Pick any place on the Moon: search 13 curated sites (south-pole candidates and Apollo references), click directly on the globe, or enter custom coordinates.
  • Set the mission: landing date and time (UTC), a mission length of 7 days, 14 days or a full 29.5-day lunar cycle, and a time step of 15, 60 or 120 minutes.
  • Size your solar panels: enter panel area and efficiency to estimate the power the site can deliver.
  • Read the results your way: a Simple mode with plain-language answers ("Daylight", "Talk to Earth", countdowns until sunset or Earthrise) and a Detailed mode with every check, percentage and value.
  • Out-of-date warning: if you change the site or any parameter after a run, Balam flags the results as outdated, so you never read stale numbers.

Timeline: time is the main control

  • Scrub or play the whole mission: drag the timeline or press play (1×, 4× or 12×) and watch light and shadow move across the terrain, with sunlight and Earth-link tracks, sunset and Earthset markers.
  • 360° horizon chart: the real horizon silhouette of the site, with the Sun and Earth at the current moment.

See it on the ground:

  • 3D globe: a Moon built entirely from NASA data, with sites colored by verdict, shadowed regions outlined, and the Sun and Earth in their real positions.
  • Horizon view: drop down to the surface and look around from the lander's point of view.
  • Landing scene: watch a landing sequence with a lander and an astronaut at the chosen site.
  • Terrain detail: a close-up 12 km patch with real slopes, shadows and adjustable vertical exaggeration.

History: keep your work:

  • Save any run with one click; star it, add notes, filter by verdict and search.
  • Reopen, duplicate and edit, or send a saved run to Compare.

Missions: learn from real landings:

  • Replay historic lunar landings: load each mission's site and landing window to see the conditions at touchdown and how Balam's verdict compares.

Built to be understood:

  • Guided onboarding: a 7-step interactive tour on first visit runs a real simulation (Apollo 11) to teach the whole flow.
  • "?" help everywhere: every term and number has a short explanation, collected in a built-in glossary.
  • "Next step" suggestions: each screen proposes the most useful next action, so you never get stuck.
  • Accessible and keyboard-friendly: full keyboard navigation and shortcuts (F for full screen, ? for help), screen-reader labels and support for reduced motion.
  • Live status: a connection indicator shows whether the data is live and retries automatically if the server drops.

Benefits

  • Turns gigabytes of raw NASA data into a visual answer that is easy to explain, in a matter of seconds.
  • Every result can be explained: users see exactly which value failed to meet its threshold, which avoids the "black box" problem in evaluation.
  • Comparing dates matters as much as comparing sites: the same site can be GO one week and NO-GO the next.
  • Works in any modern browser, with no installation, user account or API key.

Intended impact

The grazing sunlight that preserves ice at the lunar south pole makes planning power and communication systems extremely difficult. Balam makes this kind of analysis accessible. Students, teachers, science communicators and teams starting a mission can explore alternatives and technical trade-offs that until now required specialized software and expert knowledge. And through a Moon built from real NASA data, it helps the public understand why landing at the pole is so complex.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, PostgreSQL + PostGIS, SPICE kernels (DE440s/DE421, MOON_ME) with Skyfield, NASA JPL Horizons as a fallback, and digital elevation models (DEMs) in GeoTIFF format.
  • Frontend: TypeScript, React 19, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Three.js with React Three Fiber, Zustand and Vitest.
  • Lunar globe: CesiumJS, using NASA Moon Trek imagery (LROC WAC) and our own terrain tiles built from LOLA data.
  • Data: LOLA elevation models from NASA's LRO mission, LROC imagery (via Moon Trek), JPL ephemerides and a catalog of permanently shadowed regions (PSRs) on the Moon.
  • Infrastructure: our own Linux server with Docker, Woodpecker CI/CD (for testing, contract validation and automatic deployment after every merge) and Cloudflare Tunnel for public HTTPS access.
  • Process: contract-first development (OpenAPI 3.1) with a mock server, which let the frontend and backend teams work in parallel. TypeScript types are generated automatically from the contract.

Creative approach

  • Instead of a flat map full of numbers, Balam puts you at the exact spot. The lander's perspective shows the real horizon, computed from LOLA data, with the Sun and Earth moving just above it.
  • Time works as an interactive dimension: you can scrub through a week, a lunar day or a full lunar cycle as if it were a video.
  • It offers one continuous 3D experience, from the global view of the Moon down to the landing itself, with no need to jump between separate tools.
  • The name and identity come from our team, Jaguares Astrales. Balam means "jaguar" in Maya, an animal that hunts at night and can see in the dark. That makes it a fitting name for a tool designed to find light among the Moon's permanent shadows.

Factors our team considered

  • Scientific honesty: the Moon is rendered only from NASA data, and we never invent information. If ephemerides or terrain data are unavailable, the tool says so instead of showing a fictitious Sun. Example values in the documentation were replaced with real results from the API.
  • Accuracy where it really matters: we model libration, lunar curvature and the passage of the solar disk across the horizon, because at the poles even the smallest angles are decisive.
  • The right time scale: we offer 7 days, 14 days or a full 29.5-day lunar cycle, because planning a landing window and designing a mission that can survive the lunar night call for different approaches.
  • Performance: the horizon is precomputed on the server, and the timeline is sent once and replayed locally, which keeps the experience smooth in any standard browser.
  • Usability: the interface is in English and includes a 7-step guided tour, contextual help, a glossary, keyboard navigation and suggestions for the next step at every stage.
  • Open access: the tool uses only free, public NASA data, requires no private keys and credits every source within the interface.
  • Teamwork: we used a shared handoff repository where decisions and questions were recorded. This kept a distributed team aligned, a team that was also supported by AI assistants.
